title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?

paper.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference.
This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models , a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training.
Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training.
Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of 1.19 1.19 among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A central goal of generative modeling is to achieve high sample quality with efficient training and inference. Diffusion and flow-based models ( Song et al., 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2022 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities and now serve as backbones for several domains ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Abramson et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , but they rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations. This has motivated considerable effort toward one- and few-step generation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) . Much of this progress builds on diffusion and flow formulations, including consistency-based modeling ( Song et al., 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ) , flow-map learning ( Boffi et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2026b ) , and distributional distillation ( Luo et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ) . While promising, these approaches require a considerable amount of extra machinery to work, like specialized stabilization strategies, Jacobian–vector products, classifier-free guidance, a teacher to distill from, etc. A complementary approach is to train a generator by directly matching its output distribution to the data distribution. This naturally supports generation in a single network evaluation and has a long history in GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) and maximum mean discrepancy-based generators ( Li et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2017 ) . Translating these objectives into effective training, however, requires significant engineering effort ( Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Mescheder et al., 2018 ) . This latter approach has seen a recent resurgence of interest, with Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) and W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) demonstrating that direct distributional learning can produce high-quality one-step generators at scale. Their training recipes nevertheless rely on longer training-time schedules and subtle tricks like style-conditioning ( Karras et al., 2019 ) . Thus, the simplicity of one-step inference still comes at the cost of substantial complexity in getting these models to train. In this work, we therefore ask: Does training a one-step generator need to be this complicated? We introduce Priming Models , a drastically more straightforward framework for one-step generative modeling with just two basic components: [Stage 1] Reconstruction pretraining: We pretrain the network with a simple reconstruction objective – in fact, even denoising at a fixed corruption level suffices. [Stage 2] Distributional post-training: We use the pretrained network directly as a one-step generator that maps Gaussian noise to samples, then refine it by matching generated and real distributions in feature space, e.g., using an optimal transport loss. Empirically, Priming Models achieve strong performance with substantially reduced training compute across three visual domains: • ImageNet : Priming Models achieve state-of-the-art FID ( 1.19 ) 1 1 1 FD-loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) reports FID 0.72 for pixel MeanFlow by directly optimizing Fréchet Distance. We exclude this configuration from comparison and revisit this in Section 4.2 . and Fréchet distances across other feature spaces among one-step generators, outperforming Pixel MeanFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) , Drifting ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , and even multistep diffusion baseline JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , with approximately 10 × 10\times less compute than Drifting (Figure 1 , left). • Text-to-Image : Priming Models substantially outperform one-step MeanFlow on GenEval and DPG, while reducing training compute by a factor of 1.9 . • World models : Priming Models outperform the Drifting baseline ( Lu et al., 2026a ) with approximately half the training compute, while also achieving performance comparable to the (multi-step) flow matching baseline. A key factor behind our strong empirical results is that reconstruction pretraining substantially accelerates distributional post-training (Figure 1 , right). Without the former, even when the distributional objective provides useful correction directions, the network’s Jacobian may hinder how effectively the parameters update to realize these improvements. Through controlled experiments, we demonstrate that reconstruction pretraining ameliorates this by aligning the Jacobian and shaping how readily the model’s outputs can be refined. Together, our findings suggest a surprisingly minimal design principle for generative modeling: use reconstruction pretraining to prepare a generator for distributional post-training. Priming Models realize this principle, enabling high-quality one-step generators to be efficiently trained from scratch. Figure 2: One-step samples from Priming Models across three visual domains.

sections.heading: 2 Priming Models
sections.text: We first present our motivation behind Priming Models . Distributional objectives, such as Sinkhorn divergence or Wasserstein distance, offer a natural approach to one-step generative modeling by directly matching generated and real distributions. The central challenge, however, lies in translating these objectives into effective training procedures, a difficulty that helped motivate interest in alternatives such as diffusion models ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . Indeed, early maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based generators were demonstrated on relatively small datasets ( Li et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2017 ; Genevay et al., 2018 ) , while GANs have achieved high-quality generation at scale ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ; Arjovsky et al., 2017 ; Brock et al., 2018 ; Karras et al., 2019 ; Sauer et al., 2022 ) but remain sensitive to optimization ( Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Mescheder et al., 2018 ) . (a) Drifting-L (b) W-Flow XL/2 Figure 3: Fixing style embedding limits diversity (ImageNet ‘otter’, ‘arctic fox’); more samples in Appendix F.4 . More recently, Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) and W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) have achieved high-quality one-step generation on ImageNet using velocity fields trained based on kernel- and entropic OT-based distributional distances, respectively. Their reported training compute, however, remains costly; both L-size models are trained for 1,280 1{,}280 epochs, taking approximately three days on 64 NVIDIA H100 GPUs . Both also augment Gaussian inputs with learned style embeddings inspired by StyleGAN ( Karras et al., 2019 ) . We find that fixing these style embeddings yields only marginal differences between images across different Gaussian noises (Figure 3 ), although varying the style embeddings still produces diverse samples. This suggests that style conditioning is an important source of sample diversity in this setting. Taken together, these observations suggest that optimizing distributional objectives from scratch, especially without these tweaks, remains challenging. This leads us to ask: Question: Can a suitable initialization make distributional post-training more effective? Our intuition is that distributional training is challenging from scratch because at the start, the network has no information about the structure of natural images. To that end, we seek to first learn a related capability: recovering clean-image structure from corrupted inputs. Denoising reconstruction provides a natural way to learn this capability. Corrupted inputs retain information about the underlying images to guide recovery, while their clean counterparts provide direct supervision. Our hypothesis is that learning to reconstruct provides a useful initialization for subsequent distributional optimization. This motivates reconstruction pretraining as a first stage toward learning the full noise-to-image mapping.

sections.heading: 2.2 Priming Models: Understanding
sections.text: In this section, we systematically examine our intuition behind the two-stage training design of Priming Models. Figure 4 shows the online FID trajectories during post-training for models pretrained on ImageNet for 20 20 , 80 80 , and 160 160 epochs of reconstruction pretraining. It also includes a model pretrained for 160 160 epochs with a perceptual loss (Section 3.1 ), which achieves a lower FID. At a matched number of post-training updates, longer pretraining is associated with lower FID. Intuition. We posit that reconstruction pretraining captures useful structure of the data manifold, making generated samples readily correctable through parameter updates. Figure 4: Pretraining strengthens the Jacobian alignment, improving post-training efficiency. Jacobian alignment. To probe this intuition, we examine how parameter updates move generated samples in feature space. Let h θ h_{\theta} denote the feature representations of samples, and let v v be the gradient of the distributional loss in ( 2 ) with respect to h θ h_{\theta} . When the gradient aligns with directions to which J θ ​ J θ ⊤ J_{\theta}J_{\theta}^{\top} responds strongly, the resulting feature update is larger. We examine this relationship through controlled experiments below. Setup. We evaluate the four models in Figure 4 , all before post-training. For each ImageNet class and in each of the ResNet-MAE and ConvNeXt feature spaces used for distributional post-training, we collect gradients of the OT loss with respect to generated features. Across the four models, higher normalized response before post-training (x-axis) is associated with a lower online FID after post-training, consistent with our hypothesis. sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: We now demonstrate that Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training efficiency vs. generation quality across three visual domains: class-conditional generation on ImageNet (Section 3.1 ), text-to-image generation (Section 3.2 ), and world modeling (Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 ImageNet: Class-conditional generation
sections.text: Setup. We study class-conditional generation on ImageNet-1K ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. sections.heading: 3.2 Text-to-Image Generation
sections.text: We now evaluate Priming Models on text-to-image generation at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution to assess their effectiveness beyond ImageNet-scale. Setup. We build on MiniT2I ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , an open-sourced codebase for pixel-space text-to-image generation with publicly available training data. Our primary baseline is the MiniT2I MeanFlow checkpoint. For our model, we adopt the same 258 258 M-parameter MM-JiT-B/16 generator backbone. Text captions are encoded by the 341 341 M-parameter encoder of FLAN-T5-Large ( Chung et al., 2024 ) , which remains frozen throughout training. Following MiniT2I, we scale the Gaussian noise by a factor of 2, i.e., ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 2 2 ​ 𝐈 ) {\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2^{2}\mathbf{I}) , throughout training and inference. Pretraining. We first train with the reconstruction objective on CC12M ( Changpinyo et al., 2021 ) , then continue reconstruction training on a curated mixture of 120 120 k images from the codebase. Both phases use a global batch size of 1024 1024 . We use two pretraining noise configurations: a fixed corruption level s = 0.8 s=0.8 and corruption levels sampled from a reweighted logit-normal distribution p ⁡ ( s ) ∝ s − 2 ​ LogNorm ⁡ ( s , 0.8 , 0.8 2 ) p(s)\propto s^{-2}\operatorname{LogNorm}(s;0.8,0.8^{2}) . Post-training. We then post-train the model using the OT objective in ( 3 ) with ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 . At each update, we sample 64 64 distinct text captions. For each caption, we generate 32 32 samples online, applying stop-gradient to 16 16 of them. We compute the objective independently for each caption group using globally pooled features from SigLIP, ViT-MAE, and Inception-V3. For each feature branch, we normalize features by their within-batch pairwise RMS distance. Since each caption is paired with a single real image, the generated–real OT term reduces to the average squared feature distance to that image. We also replace the full ResNet-MAE and ConvNeXt feature spaces with simpler, lightweight spaces, SigLIP, Inception-V3, and ViT-MAE, keeping the same perceptual Priming-B-160 initialization and 25,000 25{,}000 OT post-training setup. Fréchet distance ( Dowson and Landau, 1982 ) is widely used to evaluate generative models, but directly optimizing it was believed to be challenging, as reliable estimation typically requires tens of thousands of samples. FD-loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) addresses this challenge by accumulating feature statistics across training steps through a feature queue or exponential moving averages, while backpropagating only through the current batch, and has demonstrated consistent improvements in pretrained one-step generators. We show that FD-loss also fits within the Priming Model framework as an alternative distributional post-training objective. Applied to the pretrained Priming-B checkpoint, it yields efficient post-training; we provide the setup and results in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generative models end-to-end. Reconstruction pretraining prepares the generator for efficient distributional post-training, enabling strong empirical performance across multiple visual domains. That said, our work leaves several open questions. Priming Models rely on pretrained feature encoders. Although we demonstrate our method with multiple sets of feature encoders, this dependence raises the question of whether it can be eliminated. The relationship between reconstruction pretraining and Jacobian alignment also warrants deeper investigation. Finally, closing the remaining performance gap with multi-step diffusion and flow models remains an important challenge. Outlook. More broadly, our results suggest that we may be overthinking the problem: the specialized formulations and elaborate training machinery used in prior work are not the only path to train one-step generators. We hope our work opens the door to simpler and more scalable approaches to one-step generative modeling.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: In this section, we review prior work on one- and few-step generative modeling, organized by their methodological category. Category 1: Trajectory straightening and flow-map learning. These lines of work obtain few-step generative models by learning from a diffusion or probability-flow trajectory. Progressive distillation repeatedly compresses a teacher sampler into fewer steps ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) . Consistency Models instead enforce agreement among predictions made at different points along the same trajectory ( Song et al., 2023 ) , while subsequent work improves their stability and scaling or extends consistency to trajectory segments ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . Rectified Flow and reflow ( Liu et al., 2023a ; Liu et al., 2023b ) seek straighter transport paths that are easier to integrate in few steps. These straightening methods modify the coupling and resulting trajectory so that coarse numerical integration can accurately reach its endpoint. A related but distinct family learns the finite-time transition across an interval of a flow-matching trajectory, such as a flow map or average velocity. This includes Flow Map Matching, Shortcut Models, MeanFlow, Improved MeanFlow, and Inductive Moment Matching ( Boffi et al., 2024 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . These methods differ in their targets and training estimators, but generally supervise a particular time-dependent transport or consistency relation. Priming: Priming Models do not attempt to recover a prescribed trajectory or flow map: reconstruction pretraining provides an initialization for the network, which we then directly use as a one-step generator. Category 2: Teacher-guided distillation. Another line of work distills a pretrained diffusion teacher into a one-step student, with much of the focus on designing effective distillation objectives. Diff-Instruct ( Luo et al., 2023 ) uses score-based distributional objectives derived from a diffusion teacher, while DMD and DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) optimize the student using the difference between teacher and student score estimates. Score Identity Distillation ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) provides a related score-based formulation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation combines score distillation with an adversarial objective to improve fidelity in the low-step regime ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) . Priming: These approaches inherit the cost and machinery required to obtain and query that teacher. In contrast, Priming Models are trained from scratch and therefore do not require a pretrained teacher. Category 3:Distributional loss (from scratch). Directly matching a generator distribution to the data distribution has a long history. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn a one-pass generator through an adversarially trained discriminator ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) , with Wasserstein objectives and regularization improving the geometry and stability of training ( Arjovsky et al., 2017 ; Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Mescheder et al., 2018 ) . Generative Moment Matching Networks use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in place of adversarial discrimination, while MMD-GANs further learn the MMD kernel adversarially ( Li et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2017 ) . Genevay et al. (2018) trains implicit generative models directly using a Sinkhorn divergence. These works, however, are limited in empirical scope and, more importantly, differ from Priming Models in that we apply the distributional objective after a reconstruction pretraining stage. Recent works revisit direct one-step learning at a more practical scale. YOSO ( Luo et al., 2024 ) stabilizes adversarial one-step training through a self-cooperative diffusion GAN, while Adversarial Flow ( Lin et al., 2025 ) trains with an adversarial objective but constrains the generator to learn the deterministic transport map associated with flow matching. Priming: Priming Models share the goal of direct distribution matching, but do not optimize it from random initialization: reconstruction pretraining first teaches the generator to correct corrupted inputs toward clean images, after which a distributional objective refines it into a one-step generator. Category 3-1: Drifting Models. Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) construct an attraction-repulsion field using a normalized Laplacian kernel and train the generator to match stop-gradient targets obtained by displacing its generated features along this field. W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) derives a training-time velocity field from the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Sinkhorn divergence, using barycentric projections computed from entropic optimal transport plans. Van Assel et al. (2026) additionally examine how the choice of frozen feature space affects transport stability in distribution matching. Priming: Priming Models introduce reconstruction pretraining before distributional optimization, and this stage is key to our strong compute vs. quality trade-off. Our implementation also seeks to dispense with the additional engineering machinery used in these works. Both reported ImageNet architectures include learned random style embeddings, and both frameworks support classifier-free guidance; Drifting additionally normalizes its constructed drift field. Priming does not use these additional mechanisms and instead optimizes an OT-based distributional surrogate. All four models reported in Section 3 share exactly the same post-training configuration, further illustrating the simplicity of our approach. This suggests that reconstruction pretraining can make distributional optimization more efficient while supporting a simpler training recipe. We hypothesize that this initialization reduces the need for additional training mechanisms, although our experiments do not isolate their individual contributions. Category 4: Distributional loss (fine-tuning). Distributional objectives have also been used to adapt pretrained generative models. MMD-DDM ( Aiello et al., 2023 ) fine-tunes pretrained diffusion models with MMD to improve quality under a restricted sampling-step budget. DiffRatio ( Chen et al., 2025 ) estimates the density ratio between noisy real and generated distributions to train a one-step model without a teacher score. FD-loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) makes feature-space Fréchet distance practical as a training objective by maintaining population-level feature statistics, and applies it to pretrained one- and multi-step generators. More recently, iRDM ( Feng et al., 2026 ) scales MMD-based post-training across multiple pretrained representation spaces. Most closely related to our work, D2O ( Zheng and Yang, 2025 ) shows that adversarial fine-tuning alone can convert a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator, while Yang et al. (2026, Section 4.3) show that FD-loss can convert JiT, a multi-step diffusion model, into a competitive one-step generator. Priming: Priming Models build on the perspective that pretraining can prepare a network for subsequent distributional optimization. We investigate how simple this pretraining task can be, showing that reconstruction—even denoising at a single fixed noise level without noise-level conditioning—can provide an effective initialization for our distributional training, despite poor initial one-step samples (Figure 1 , right). We further examine alternative pretraining tasks (Section 4.1 ) within the same framework. Finally, viewing reconstruction pretraining and distributional post-training as a complete training procedure also enables comparisons with prior methods based on total training compute across both stages, measured in EFLOPs.

sections.heading: E.1 FD-loss Objective
sections.text: FD-loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) directly compares the generated and real feature distributions through their first two moments. Let ϕ \phi be a frozen feature encoder, and let q θ ϕ := ϕ # ​ q θ q_{\theta}^{\phi}:=\phi_{\#}q_{\theta} and p ϕ := ϕ # ​ p p^{\phi}:=\phi_{\#}p denote the generated and real feature distributions, respectively. Denoting their means and covariances as ( μ q , Σ q ) (\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q}) and ( μ p , Σ p ) (\mu_{p},\Sigma_{p}) , the objective is the squared Fréchet distance between the corresponding moment-matched Gaussian distributions ( Dowson and Landau, 1982 ) : ℱ FD ​ ( q θ ϕ , p ϕ ) := ∥ μ q − μ p ∥ 2 2 + Tr ⁡ ( Σ q + Σ p − 2 ​ ( Σ p 1 / 2 ​ Σ q ​ Σ p 1 / 2 ) 1 / 2 ) . \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{FD}}(q_{\theta}^{\phi},p^{\phi}):=\lVert\mu_{q}-\mu_{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\Sigma_{q}+\Sigma_{p}-2\bigl(\Sigma_{p}^{1/2}\Sigma_{q}\Sigma_{p}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}\right). (14) Equivalently, Equation ( 14 ) is the squared 2 2 -Wasserstein distance between 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ q , Σ q ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q}) and 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ p , Σ p ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{p},\Sigma_{p}) . Unlike the objectives for Sinkhorn divergence or MMD, ℱ FD \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{FD}} is minimized directly: there is no generated self-interaction term or independent generated reference batch. Gradients propagate through the generated moments ( μ q , Σ q ) (\mu_{q},\Sigma_{q}) to q θ q_{\theta} , whereas the real moments ( μ p , Σ p ) (\mu_{p},\Sigma_{p}) are fixed. In practice, FD-loss replaces the population moments with accumulated estimates so that the objective can be optimized without placing the full feature population in a single minibatch ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . FD-loss performs marginal matching instead of conditional distribution matching.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.20331v1 [cs.LG] 14 Oct 2026 Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation? Woobin Park Jaeyeon Kim Yilun Du Sitan Chen Bohyung Han Affiliation: Seoul National University Affiliation: Harvard University ⋆ Equal contribution Summer 2026 Abstract Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models , a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at 256 × 256 256	imes 256 resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of 1.19 1.19 among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming . Figure 1: Priming Models dramatically improve the training compute vs. FID trade-off on ImageNet ( left ). Simple reconstruction pretraining provides an effective initialization that makes subsequent distributional post-training substantially more efficient ( right ). 1 Introduction A central goal of generative modeling is to achieve high sample quality with efficient training and inference. Diffusion and flow-based models ( Song et al., 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2022 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities and now serve as backbones for several domains ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Abramson et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , but they rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations. This has motivated considerable effort toward one- and few-step generation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) . Much of this progress builds on diffusion and flow formulations, including consistency-based modeling ( Song et al., 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ) , flow-map learning ( Boffi et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2026b ) , and distributional distillation ( Luo et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ) . While promising, these approaches require a considerable amount of extra machinery to work, like specialized stabilization strategies, Jacobian–vector products, classifier-free guidance, a teacher to distill from, etc. A complementary approach is to train a generator by directly matching its output distribution to the data distribution. This naturally supports generation in a single network evaluation and has a long history in GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) and maximum mean discrepancy-based generators ( Li et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2017 ) . Translating these objectives into effective training, however, requires significant engineering effort ( Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Mescheder et al., 2018 ) . This latter approach has seen a recent resurgence of interest, with Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) and W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) demonstrating that direct distributional learning can produce high-quality one-step generators at scale. Their training recipes nevertheless rely on longer training-time schedules and subtle tricks like style-conditioning ( Karras et al., 2019 ) . Thus, the simplicity of one-step inference still comes at the cost of substantial complexity in getting these models to train. In this work, we therefore ask: Does training a one-step generator need to be this complicated? We introduce Priming Models , a drastically more straightforward framework for one-step generative modeling with just two basic components: [Stage 1] Reconstruction pretraining: We pretrain the network with a simple reconstruction objective – in fact, even denoising at a fixed corruption level suffices. [Stage 2] Distributional post-training: We use the pretrained network directly as a one-step generator that maps Gaussian noise to samples, then refine it by matching generated and real distributions in feature space, e.g., using an optimal transport loss. Empirically, Priming Models achieve strong performance with substantially reduced training compute across three visual domains: • ImageNet : Priming Models achieve state-of-the-art FID ( 1.19 ) 1 1 1 FD-loss ( Yang et al., 2026 ) reports FID 0.72 for pixel MeanFlow by directly optimizing Fréchet Distance. We exclude this configuration from comparison and revisit this in Section 4.2 . and Fréchet distances across other feature spaces among one-step generators, outperforming Pixel MeanFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) , Drifting ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , and even multistep diffusion baseline JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , with approximately 10 × 10	imes less compute than Drifting (Figure 1 , left). • Text-to-Image : Priming Models substantially outperform one-step MeanFlow on GenEval and DPG, while reducing training compute by a factor of 1.9 . • World models : Priming Models outperform the Drifting baseline ( Lu et al., 2026a ) with approximately half the training compute, while also achieving performance comparable to the (multi-step) flow matching baseline. A key factor behind our strong empirical results is that reconstruction pretraining substantially accelerates distributional post-training (Figure 1 , right). Without the former, even when the distributional objective provides useful correction directions, the network’s Jacobian may hinder how effectively the parameters update to realize these improvements. Through controlled experiments, we demonstrate that reconstruction pretraining ameliorates this by aligning the Jacobian and shaping how readily the model’s outputs can be refined. Together, our findings suggest a surprisingly minimal design principle for generative modeling: use reconstruction pretraining to prepare a generator for distributional post-training. Priming Models realize this principle, enabling high-quality one-step generators to be efficiently trained from scratch. Figure 2: One-step samples from Priming Models across three visual domains. 2 Priming Models We first present our motivation behind Priming Models . Distributional objectives, such as Sinkhorn divergence or Wasserstein distance, offer a natural approach to one-step generative modeling by directly matching generated and real distributions. The central challenge, however, lies in translating these objectives into effective training procedures, a difficulty that helped motivate interest in alternatives such as diffusion models ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . Indeed, early maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based generators were demonstrated on relatively small datasets ( Li et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2017 ; Genevay et al., 2018 ) , while GANs have achieved high-quality generation at scale ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ; Arjovsky et al., 2017 ; Brock et al., 2018 ; Karras et al., 2019 ; Sauer et al., 2022 ) but remain sensitive to optimization ( Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Mescheder et al., 2018 ) . (a) Drifting-L (b) W-Flow XL/2 Figure 3: Fixing style embedding limits diversity (ImageNet ‘otter’, ‘arctic fox’); more samples in Appendix F.4 . More recently, Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) and W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) have achieved high-quality one-step generation on ImageNet using velocity fields trained based on kernel- and entropic OT-based distributional distances, respectively. Their reported training compute, however, remains costly; both L-size models are trained for 1,280 1{,}280 epochs, taking approximately three days on 64 NVIDIA H100 GPUs . Both also augment Gaussian inputs with learned style embeddings inspired by StyleGAN ( Karras et al., 2019 ) . We find that fixing these style embeddings yields only marginal differences between images across different Gaussian noises (Figure 3 ), although varying the style embeddings still produces diverse samples. This suggests that style conditioning is an important source of sample diversity in this setting. Taken together, these observations suggest that optimizing distributional objectives from scratch, especially without these tweaks, remains challenging. This leads us to ask: Question: Can a suitable initialization make distributional post-training more effective? Our intuition is that distributional training is challenging from scratch because at the start, the network has no information about the structure of natural images. To that end, we seek to first learn a related capability: recovering clean-image structure from corrupted inputs. Denoising reconstruction provides a natural way to learn this capability. Corrupted inputs retain information about the underlying images to guide recovery, while their clean counterparts provide direct supervision. Our hypothesis is that learning to reconstruct provides a useful initialization for subsequent distributional optimization. This motivates reconstruction pretraining as a first stage toward learning the full noise-to-image mapping. 2.1 Priming Models: Training recipe Building on this intuition, Priming Models train a one-step generator in two stages: reconstruction pretraining and distributional post-training.
